title: Glossary
markdown:
The terms from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **.bss** | The section of zeroed space reserved with resb and friends. (1.05) |
| **%rep** | Repeats a block of code a number of times at assembly time. (7.02) |
| **Accumulator** | A register that collects a running total; several independent ones let additions overlap. (6.03) |
| **Address** | The number of a byte in memory. A label is one. (1.05, 4.01) |
| **Addressing mode** | A way to form an address: base + index × scale + displacement, or relative to rip. (4.01) |
| **Alignment** | Being at an address that is a multiple of some size; the stack must be 16-aligned at a call. (5.02) |
| **Anonymous mapping** | Memory from mmap that is not backed by a file, always zero-filled (8.04) |
| **argc and argv** | The argument count and the pointers to the argument strings, on the stack at _start (8.05) |
| **ARM64** | The instruction set of phones and Apple-chip Macs: 31 registers, fixed 4-byte instructions, load-store. (6.05) |
| **Assembler** | The program that turns assembly into machine code: NASM here. (1.01) |
| **AT&T syntax** | The other way of writing x86 assembly, source first: `movl $1, %eax`. GCC's default. (1.01, 5.05) |
| **AVX** | Wider SIMD with 256-bit ymm and 512-bit zmm registers. (6.04) |
| **Backtrace** | The chain of return addresses on the stack, as a debugger shows it. (5.01) |
| **Branch prediction** | The processor guessing which way a jump will go and working ahead. (3.05) |
| **Callee-saved** | Registers a function must give back unchanged: rbx, rbp, rsp, r12 to r15. (5.02) |
| **Caller-saved** | Registers any call may change: rax, rcx, rdx, rsi, rdi, r8 to r11. (5.02) |
| **Calling convention** | The agreement on where arguments and results go and which registers survive a call. (5.02) |
| **Carry flag (CF)** | Set when an unsigned result wrapped around. (2.04) |
| **cmov** | A conditional move: copies only if a condition holds, with no jump. (3.05) |
| **comisd** | Compares two doubles and sets the flags like an unsigned comparison. (7.01) |
| **Compare-and-swap** | `lock cmpxchg`: stores a new value only if memory still holds the expected one. (7.05) |
| **cqo** | Fills rdx with the sign of rax, before idiv. (2.02) |
| **cvtsd2si** | Converts a double to an integer, rounding to the nearest (ties to even). (7.01) |
| **cvttsd2si** | Converts a double to an integer, cutting the fraction off. (7.01) |
| **Debugger** | A program that runs another one step by step: gdb, lldb, WinDbg. (6.05) |
| **Dependency chain** | Instructions that each need the previous result, so they cannot overlap. (6.03) |
| **Direction flag** | The flag that makes string instructions move forwards (clear, with cld) or backwards (8.01) |
| **Directive** | An instruction to the assembler, not the processor: db, section, global, equ. (1.05) |
| **Displacement** | The constant part of an address. (4.01) |
| **ELF** | The file format of Linux programs. (1.01) |
| **Environment** | The NAME=value strings a program receives, stored after argv on the stack at _start (8.05) |
| **Epilogue** | The end of a function that undoes its prologue: leave, ret. (5.03) |
| **equ** | Names a constant number. (1.05) |
| **Exit code** | The number a program hands to the exit system call; 0 means success. (1.03) |
| **File descriptor** | A small number the kernel gives for an open file, used by read, write and close. (7.03) |
| **Flags** | Single bits in rflags recording facts about the last result: ZF, SF, CF, OF. (2.04) |
| **Frame** | A function call's part of the stack: return address, saved registers, locals. (5.03) |
| **Horizontal sum** | Adding up the lanes of a SIMD register. (6.04) |
| **Immediate** | A constant written in an instruction: `mov eax, 42`. (1.03) |
| **Indirect call** | A call to the address held in a register or memory, such as call rax (8.03) |
| **Intel syntax** | Destination first, no prefixes: `mov eax, 1`. Used by NASM and this course. (1.01) |
| **istruc** | Lays out an initialised record in data, with `at` placing each field. (7.04) |
| **Jump table** | An array of addresses for an indirect jump: a fast switch. (3.04) |
| **Kernel** | The core of the operating system, reached by system calls. (1.04) |
| **Label** | A name for an address. (1.01) |
| **Lane** | One of the values side by side in a SIMD register. (6.04) |
| **lea** | Load effective address: computes an address without reading memory. (4.01) |
| **Leaf function** | A function that calls no other functions. (5.02) |
| **Linker** | Joins object files into a program: ld here. (1.01) |
| **Little-endian** | Storing the lowest byte of a number first, as x86 does. (1.05) |
| **Local label** | A label starting with a dot, belonging to the label above it. (3.01) |
| **lock prefix** | Makes a read-modify-write instruction atomic across cores. (7.05) |
| **Machine code** | The bytes a processor runs. (1.01) |
| **Macro** | A named piece of code the NASM preprocessor expands where it is used (`%define`, `%macro`). (7.02) |
| **Macro-local label** | A label written `%%name` inside a macro, renamed at each use so it never clashes. (7.02) |
| **Magic number** | A constant that replaces division by a fixed number with a multiply and a shift (8.02) |
| **Magic number division** | Dividing by a constant by multiplying with its reciprocal and shifting. (6.01) |
| **mmap** | The system call that maps new memory (or a file) into the program; 9 on Linux x86-64 (8.04) |
| **Mnemonic** | An instruction's name, such as mov or add. (1.01) |
| **NASM** | The Netwide Assembler, used in this course. (1.01) |
| **Negative error** | A failed system call returns minus the error number, such as -2 for no such file. (7.03) |
| **Open flags** | Bits ORed into open's second argument: read/write mode, create, truncate, append. (7.03) |
| **Overflow flag (OF)** | Set when a signed result is wrong because it did not fit. (2.04) |
| **popcnt** | Counts the 1 bits of a value. (7.05) |
| **Prologue** | The start of a function that builds its frame: push rbp, mov rbp, rsp. (5.03) |
| **Red zone** | 128 bytes below rsp that a leaf function may use on Linux. (5.02) |
| **Register** | A small storage slot inside the processor. (1.02) |
| **rep** | A prefix that repeats a string instruction rcx times; repe and repne also stop on a comparison (8.01) |
| **Return address** | The address call pushes and ret jumps back to. (5.01) |
| **rip** | The instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction. (1.02) |
| **RISC-V** | An open instruction set in the load-store style. (6.05) |
| **rsp** | The stack pointer: the address of the top of the stack. (4.04) |
| **Saturation** | Arithmetic that stops at the largest or smallest value instead of wrapping. (6.04) |
| **Scalar double** | One 64-bit floating-point value in an xmm register; instructions ending in `sd` work on it. (7.01) |
| **Section** | A part of the program: .text, .data, .rodata, .bss. (1.05) |
| **setcc** | Sets a byte to 1 or 0 by a condition. (3.05) |
| **Shadow space** | 32 bytes a caller reserves on the stack in the Windows convention. (5.05) |
| **Sign flag (SF)** | Set when a result's top bit is 1. (2.04) |
| **SIMD** | Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction working on several lanes. (6.04) |
| **Spinlock** | A lock taken by looping until an atomic exchange finds it free. (7.05) |
| **Stack** | Memory that grows downwards, used for return addresses, saved registers and locals. (4.04) |
| **Stack overflow** | Running past the end of the stack, usually by recursing too deep. (5.04) |
| **String instruction** | movsb, stosb, lodsb, scasb or cmpsb: one step of a loop over memory using rsi, rdi and rcx (8.01) |
| **struc** | Defines named field offsets and a size for a record, without reserving memory. (7.04) |
| **Structure of arrays** | Keeping each field of many records in its own array, good for loops over one field. (7.04) |
| **System call** | A request to the operating system with the syscall instruction. (1.04) |
| **System V AMD64** | The calling convention of Linux and macOS. (5.02) |
| **Tail call** | Ending a function with jmp to another function, so that one returns straight to our caller (8.03) |
| **Two's complement** | The way negative numbers are stored, which lets one add serve signed and unsigned. (2.01) |
| **tzcnt** | Counts the 0 bits below the lowest 1 (64 for zero); `bsf` gives the same position but is undefined for zero. (7.05) |
| **Unrolling** | Doing several rounds of a loop's work per jump. (6.03) |
| **x86-64** | The 64-bit instruction set of most PCs and servers, also called x64 and AMD64. (1.01) |
| **xmm register** | One of the 16 SSE registers used for floating point and SIMD; `xmm0` returns a double. (7.01) |
| **xmm registers** | The 16 SIMD registers of 128 bits. (6.04) |
| **Zero flag (ZF)** | Set when a result is 0. (2.04) |
